statement: For a self-paced /loop (no interval given), Claude ends the loop by calling ScheduleWakeup with stop: true. statement: Claude Code added the `sandbox.filesystem.disabled` setting in v2.1.216 (released 2026-07-20). When set to `true`, the sandbox skips filesystem isolation while keeping network isolation, so sandboxed commands get unrestricted host filesystem read/write but egress stays confined to allowed domains. It is honored only from user settings, managed settings, or the `--settings` CLI flag; project `.claude/settings.json`/`.local.json` cannot set it. When managed settings configure any `sandbox.filesystem` key or list any `sandbox.credentials.files` entry, only managed settings can set it, and when `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB` is set Claude Code ignores it from every source and keeps filesystem isolation on.
applicability: Claude Code v2.1.216+ CLI, sandbox enabled (macOS/Linux/WSL2)
candidate_guidance: Treat filesystem.disabled as a network-only isolation mode and do not enable it for untrusted workloads: with auto-allow a sandboxed command can write shell startup files, $PATH executables, or settings and escalate its own access on the next run. Prefer keeping both layers on; if used, restrict it to managed settings.

statement: Claude Code added the `sandbox.network.strictAllowlist` setting in v2.1.219 (released 2026-07-24). When set to `true`, the sandbox denies sandboxed commands access to any host outside the allowlist instead of prompting for approval. The allowlist is `allowedDomains` plus domains from `WebFetch(domain:...)` allow rules, or only the managed-settings entries when `allowManagedDomainsOnly` is set. It is honored only from user, managed, or CLI `--settings` settings (repository `.claude/settings.json`/`.local.json` have no effect) and applies to sandboxed Bash commands only; in-process tools such as WebFetch still follow their own permission rules.
applicability: Claude Code v2.1.219+ CLI, sandbox enabled
candidate_guidance: Use strictAllowlist to convert the default prompt-on-new-host behavior into hard deny-by-default egress for unattended sandboxed runs. It must be set in user or managed settings; a project-level setting is ignored.

statement: OWASP MCP Security Cheat Sheet (accessed 2026-07-30) Best Practices section 3 'Sandbox and Isolate MCP Servers' recommends running local MCP servers in sandboxed environments (containers, chroot, application sandboxes), restricting filesystem access to only required directories, disabling network access unless explicitly needed, using stdio transport for local servers to limit access to the MCP client, and separating sensitive servers (payment, auth, PII) from general-purpose ones. statement: The OWASP MCP Security Cheat Sheet (accessed 2026-07-30) recommends, for MCP authentication and least privilege: OAuth 2.0 with PKCE for remote-server authorization flows; scoped per-server credentials that are never shared across servers, with narrow OAuth scopes; storing OAuth tokens in OS-native secure credential storage (the cheat sheet names macOS Keychain, Windows Credential Manager, and Linux Secret Service) and never in plaintext config files; preferring short-lived ephemeral tokens over long-lived personal access tokens; and validating on each request that the session or token belongs to the current requester to prevent confused-deputy abuse, since the MCP server otherwise acts with its own often-broad privileges.

statement: Per the Claude Code hooks reference (PreToolUse decision control), a PreToolUse hook that emits hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision "allow" skips the permission prompt (auto-approves the tool call) — except for tools that require user interaction and connector tools an organization set to "ask" — and valid values are allow/deny/ask/defer. However, the claim's assertion that a hook's decision 'takes precedence over settings-based permission rules' is NOT what the reference says: it states verbatim 'Deny and ask rules are still evaluated regardless of what the hook returns.' A hook can tighten (a 'deny' overrides a settings allow), but a hook 'allow' does NOT override settings deny or ask rules.
applicability: Claude Code hooks (PreToolUse), vendor docs current as of 2026-07-30
candidate_guidance: A hook 'allow' silently skips the interactive prompt only for tools not already gated by a deny/ask rule (or user-interaction/org-ask connectors), so an installed hook can grant execution without a prompt for otherwise-ungated tools. But it CANNOT bypass settings deny/ask rules, which are still evaluated regardless of the hook. Therefore an out-of-model settings deny rule (e.g. denying network/exfil commands) IS a reliable floor that a malicious hook's 'allow' cannot override — prefer deny/ask rules as the guardrail. Still treat installed hooks as fully privileged code, since a hook is arbitrary shell that can independently rewrite settings files (see PromptArmor, reddit-lane-15).
